metadata.title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume V): Learning Strategies and Attitudes for Life

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports results from the OECD PISA 2022 assessment, which is implemented using a complex, multi-stage sampling design at the student, school, and country/economy levels. In PISA, analyses of student outcomes are typically conducted with sampling weights to ensure population-representative estimates within each participating system, and (where applicable) replicate weights to support correct uncertainty estimation under the complex design. This specific excerpt does not provide the exact weight variable names or replicate-weight scheme used in the reported tables/figures, so the precise implementation details cannot be extracted here. For users re-analyzing PISA 2022 microdata, the recommended approach is to apply the official PISA sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) and to use the PISA scaling/scoring documentation for the relevant constructs.

The excerpt does not report a PV estimation or combining procedure (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or any missing-data imputation/deletion strategy for an analytic model. sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available PISA 2022 assessment sample for the participating OECD Member and partner economies referenced in the volume (the excerpt reports nearly 700 000 students from 81 participating economies). No additional analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., grade-only, module-only, or complete-case rules) are specified in the provided text.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume synthesizes PISA 2022 results on learning strategies and attitudes for life, alongside contextual findings about performance, equity, and resilience during and after COVID-19 disruptions. The excerpt states that nearly 700 000 students from 81 OECD Member and partner economies participated in PISA 2022, making it the first large-scale study to collect data on performance, well-being, and equity before and after COVID-19 disruptions. The report highlights cross-system comparisons (e.g., stability vs declines relative to PISA 2018), and it discusses relationships between reported technology use, teacher support, parental engagement, and mathematics outcomes, including equity considerations. Because this excerpt is not an empirical modeling paper, it does not specify the PV/scaling and missing-data procedures used for any particular statistical model, nor does it report ML model performance metrics. Consequently, the methodological details required to reproduce the exact estimates are not extractable from the provided text alone.
